implementation_notes: The Swift standard library has no bounded blocking queue: AsyncStream buffers, but its documented default limit is Int.max and its buffering policies keep or drop the newest/oldest elements - dropping is shedding, the opposite of levelling. The honest realization is therefore hand-written: an actor owns the pending array and a list of CheckedContinuation waiters; push hands the job to a waiter if one is parked (or buffers it up to capacity) and pop suspends with withCheckedContinuation when the buffer is empty. Consumers are a TaskGroup iterating an AsyncStream or looping over pop(); because actors are reentrant, capacity and waiter checks must happen in the same synchronous section as the state change.
pitfalls: Actor reentrancy: any await between a capacity check and the state change lets another task interleave, so the bound must be enforced in one synchronous step or with an explicit backpressure continuation.
AsyncStream's default buffer is unbounded and its policies drop elements; neither levels load by itself.
Forgetting to resume every stored continuation (on cancellation or shutdown) leaks waiting tasks forever; onTermination/cancellation must resume them.
A TaskGroup whose child tasks never return prevents the parent scope from completing - workers need a termination signal such as closing the stream.

variants.name: AsyncChannel from swift-async-algorithms
variants.implementation_notes: Apple's swift-async-algorithms package provides AsyncChannel, described as an asynchronous sequence with back-pressure sending semantics: send suspends while the consumer is behind, which is exactly the bounded hand-off, delivered as a maintained package rather than hand-written actor code. Consumers are for-await loops, typically one per task in a TaskGroup for parallel draining, and finish() ends the sequence. Choose it when the project already depends on the package or when a hand-written continuation buffer is judged riskier than a dependency; the stdlib-only project keeps the actor variant.
variants.idiom_name: AsyncChannel with for-await consumers in a TaskGroup
pitfalls: It is a package dependency, not the standard library; version readiness and platform minimums must be part of the decision.
Sendable requirements propagate: jobs crossing the channel must be Sendable, or the compiler rejects the concurrency.
Without finish() the for-await loops never end and the TaskGroup never completes.
